body_markdown:
Tucked inside a press release celebrating the one-millionth BMW M model is a status update on the all-electric M3. The takeaway? The arrival of this controversial M3 variant is very close indeed.


For starters, BMW is sharing full-body photos of a car and clearly identifying it as a pre-production version of the all-electric M3. Apparently, it is known as Future Project. Leave it to the Germans to come up with impenetrably mysterious, obscure names for their future projects! As teasers go, this one is pretty obvious: The car isn’t wearing any of the bulky camo that manufacturers use to obscure the surfacing and proportions of a vehicle. The livery is an abstract pattern that’s part camo,[part art car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/warhol-painted-bmw-m1-added-to-national-historic-vehicle-register/) , and said livery doesn’t leave much to the imagination.


BMW M


Set this pre-production M3 against[the BMW M Concept Neue Klasse concept from June](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bmw-m-concept-neue-klasse-pictures/) , and you’ll have to look closely indeed to find the differences. The two display the same proportions, with a sloping nose, small kidney “grilles,” prominent wheel arches, and a stubby decklid. They also wear very similar wheels, with a sort of spiderweb-looking design. The stacked pair of square lights on each corner of the car—BMW calls them “Track Lights”—carry over to the production car, as BMW promised.

The BMW M Concept Neue Klasse.


The differences lie in the details. The ducktail spoiler from the concept is gone, with its cut-out above the BMW roundel, which the concept placed on a protruding vertical bit between the skinny taillights. So is the rear air diffuser, at least in its exact form. As you’d expect, the door handles and side-view mirrors of the production version differ from the concept:[Like its 3 Series brethren](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/the-2027-bmw-3-series-were-most-excited-to-drive-isnt-the-ev-or-the-m3/) , the forthcoming M3 will use flush-mounted door handles. This pre-production example also appears to use normal, five-lug wheels rather than the concept’s centerlocks.


BMW M


The new, battery-electric M3 will probably use some kind of active aero in the front, judging by the horizontal vanes you can see behind the lower part of the front fascia (see the photo at the top of this article). Minimizing drag is a high priority when engineering an electric vehicle, because it directly impacts the efficiency (and range) of the driveline. However, you’ve got to balance drag against cooling, which EVs—especially performance-oriented ones—do need (though less than their ICE brethren). We’d expect these vanes to remain closed for low-intensity driving and to open up when the driver gets more aggressive, and the motors (and/or brakes) need a little extra airflow to maintain maximum performance.


The all-electric version of the M3 will be produced at BMW’s “flagship” plant in Munich. (As you may remember from last year, BMW said that it will also offer a six-cylinder version, “because,” they said, “we understand it may be early for some committed M fans to make the switch.”) Beginning next year, the Munich facility will produce only all-electric models, and based on the caption below, we are pretty sure the battery-powered M3 will be among them. Stay tuned!
